references.title: Ten simple rules for structuring papers
references.note: Practitioner rules, not tested: one central contribution in the title, context-content-conclusion at every scale, the abstract as broad-narrow-broad.

references.authors: International Committee of Medical Journal Editors
references.title: Preparing a Manuscript for Submission to a Medical Journal
references.note: Editors' standard for biomedical journals: what each IMRaD part and a structured abstract hold; authors must verify that references support their statements.

references.title: Grant proposals (or give me the money!)
references.note: University handout: write for a colleague who knows the field, follow the guidelines exactly, expect selective reading.

references.title: Business writing
references.note: University handout: audience questions, the OABC pattern, concise is not blunt; states no bottom-line-first rule.

references.authors: Takako Kojima and Helena A. Popiel
references.title: Effective use of hedging in scientific manuscripts: advice to non-native English-speaking researchers
references.note: Advice with before-and-after examples; calibrate hedges to the evidence. No data on how readers judge hedged claims.

references.authors: George D. Gopen and Judith A. Swan
references.title: The Science of Scientific Writing (American Scientist, reprint)
references.note: Expert essay with author-judged rewrites, no experiment: put old information first and new information last, keep subject and verb close; the principles are not rules.

references.title: Ten simple rules for writing a literature review
references.note: Practitioner rules, not tested: a review is critical, not stamp collecting; record the search; IMRaD rarely suits a review.

references.title: Current findings from research on structured abstracts: an update
references.note: A non-systematic, opinion-style review; structured abstracts are reported to be more complete and clear, judged mostly by undergraduates.

references.title: Executive summary
references.note: Weak evidence, used only to name the genre: an executive summary conveys the essence, may run to 500 words, and tends to be written last.

references.authors: National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIH)
references.title: Write your research plan
references.note: Funder guidance: the aims page is a capsule of the plan; the review framework changed in 2025, so check current limits.

references.authors: Luciana B. Sollaci and Mauricio G. Pereira
references.title: The introduction, methods, results, and discussion (IMRAD) structure: a fifty-year survey
references.note: A count of 1,297 articles in four medical journals, 1935 to 1985: IMRaD went from rare to universal in original papers; not to be extrapolated beyond those journals.

references.title: Abstracts
references.note: University writing-centre handout: selection and indexing; descriptive against informative abstracts; word counts are rules of thumb.

references.title: Scientific abstracts and plain language summaries in psychology: a comparison based on readability indices
references.note: 103 pairs: plain language summaries scored better on four readability indices; comprehension was not tested.

references.title: Argument
references.note: University handout: a claim backed by evidence; evidence norms differ by field; one or two serious counterarguments in depth.

references.title: Writing for understanding
references.note: Active voice, present tense and hidden verbs, with detection signals; house guidance without tests. The capture is partial.

references.title: Literature reviews
references.note: University handout: summary plus synthesis, organised around ideas, with the organising principle stated.

references.title: Confabulated references in the age of AI: contamination of the biomedical scientific literature
references.note: An editorial that collects reported cases of invented references; its figures are secondhand from a few small studies.

references.authors: National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIH)
references.title: Draft specific aims
references.note: Funder guidance: two to four aims, usually three, finishable in the funding period, with endpoints; do not be overly ambitious. Some NIAID content is no longer updated.

references.title: Parts of a memo
references.note: University guide: heading, opening, summary, discussion, closing, attachments; a specific, concise subject line.

references.title: Audience and purpose (memos)
references.note: University guide: send a memo only to those who need it; use a call or meeting for what is too sensitive to write.

references.title: Progress reports
references.note: Weak evidence, used only to name the genre: completed work, a plan for the rest, and challenges.

references.title: Proposals
references.note: Weak evidence, used only to name the genre: a problem, solutions and costs, with qualifications and a budget.
